# Cup Day, the Coolroom and 14 Bags of Ice

Jonno,

You keep asking what happened with the coolroom on Cup Day, so here you go. I’m putting it on the blog so I only have to tell you once. Also Mum reads this and she’ll be glad to know what I’ve been doing instead of calling her back.

First off, you would’ve cried. London has made you soft. You’ve probably got a nice little kitchen over there where the fridges work and everyone says “heard” without throwing a tea towel. Come back for one Melbourne Cup service and we’ll see how long that lasts.

I got in at 6.40 on Tuesday morning and opened the coolroom to find it was 11 degrees. Eleven. The compressor had died sometime overnight and everything in there had been sitting around having a lovely time getting warm.

We had 140 covers booked for lunch. Set menu, three courses. Raff was away for Cup Day, so I was running the kitchen.

I called Wally from Coldline, who told me he couldn’t get out until Wednesday because the part was coming from Sydney. Fair enough, not his fault, but not what you want to hear while standing in a coolroom that feels like a slightly chilly bedroom.

Phil’s contribution was “just make it work mate.”

Cheers, Phil. Hadn’t thought of that. I was going to lie down on the floor and wait for the beef to cook itself, but now that you’ve said that we’re sorted.

We lost about $1,800 worth of stock, mostly dairy and the duck legs. There was a fair bit of staring into the coolroom doing maths nobody wanted to do. Then we had to get moving, because the bookings weren’t going anywhere and Wally’s part wasn’t magically arriving from Sydney.

Everything we could save got crammed into the two undercounters and the bar fridge. Marta from the cafe next door let us use half her walk-in, which was extremely decent of her considering we turned up asking to move half a bistro into it on Cup morning.

She’s making us pay her back in croissant credit. I reckon I owe her about three weeks of staff meal at this point. Every time I see her she gives me a look like she’s checking the balance.

The best part was me and Benny taking 30 kilos of beef shin down the laneway on a milk crate trolley. In the rain, obviously. Wouldn’t have been much of a story if it was sunny and the trolley had all its wheels.

One wheel came off halfway down. Just came off. So there we were trying to keep the beef on the trolley while dragging the bloody thing through the laneway to Marta’s. Benny was not enjoying himself. I was being very calm and professional, as you know I always am.

A lady on table 9 must’ve seen us through the window because later she asked if the beef was “free range from the laneway.” Fair question. I’m just glad she didn’t see what we looked like trying to get it there.

Kev, meanwhile, took the old esky and filled it with ice from the servo. Fourteen bags. The bloke at the servo asked if we were having a party, which is technically one way to describe Cup Day at the bistro. Kev came back with enough ice to make the esky useful and probably put the servo guy’s kids through uni.

You remember that old esky. The one that looks like it’s been dropped off a moving ute. Turns out we’d just been waiting for its big day.

By the time service was getting close, every fridge had something in it that didn’t belong there, Marta had half our kitchen next door, and we were trying to remember where we’d put everything. You would’ve been furious. Actually, you would’ve been furious for the first half hour and then started giving the bar fridge a name.

At 12.15 we had to 86 the panna cotta. Bit late to be changing dessert, but there wasn’t much choice. So dessert became “affogato with whatever,” which is not how I’d usually describe a menu item to paying customers, but it covers the situation.

And people loved it more. Of course they did. We spend time getting the panna cotta right and the dessert they’re happy about is coffee and whatever we could put with it.

I’m still annoyed about that, actually.

The weird thing is, once service started, everyone was completely locked in. Benny stopped swearing at the trolley long enough to cook, Kev kept the ice situation under control, and we got through the 140 covers. People helped each other out, nobody stood around waiting to be told what to do, and somehow it was honestly the best service we did all year.

Not that I’m telling Phil that. He’ll take it as proof that “just make it work mate” is a plan and next Cup Day he’ll unplug the coolroom himself.

Oh, and my horse in the sweep was called **Ice Cold Lad**. Came second last. Even the horse was taking the piss.

Anyway, that’s what happened. The coolroom died, the trolley died, the panna cotta died, and somehow lunch was good. Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite.

You would’ve loved it, right up until the wheel fell off. Then you would’ve cried.

Come home ya flog.
